yoma-9b-14-14.note: Reish Lakish was swimming in the Jordan River when Rabba bar bar Hana came and gave him a hand. Reish Lakish said to him: 'My God! I hate you,' meaning the Jews of Babylonia. He explained with a verse from the Song of Songs: had all of them come up to the Land of Israel together, like a wall, in the days of Ezra, they would have been like silver, which rot cannot touch. Because they came only partly, like doors, they are like cedar, which rot does attack.
yoma-9b-14-14.why: The Gemara has been asking whether the generations of the First or the Second Temple were greater. Reish Lakish's outburst explains why the Second Temple fell short: not all the exiles returned. The Gemara then doubts he would have spoken with Rabba bar bar Hana at all.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel, swimming in the Jordan, who rebuked the Babylonian Jews.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who gave Reish Lakish a hand out of the river.

terms.meaning: The time when exiles came back from Babylonia to the Land of Israel and built the Second Temple; many stayed behind.
God's presence dwelling among the people, which the translation says was only partly felt in the Second Temple.

yoma-11a-5-5.note: Rabbi Yehuda told of an examiner who was checking mezuzot in the upper market of Tzippori, when a Roman official caught him and fined him a thousand zuz. The Gemara asks: did not Rabbi Elazar say that people on their way to do a commandment come to no harm? It answers that where the danger is constant, one may not rely on that, just as Samuel feared Saul would kill him, even when God sent him.
yoma-11a-5-5.why: Abaye has explained that the gates of Mehoza had no mezuza because of the danger from the gentiles living there. Rabbi Yehuda's incident shows that checking public mezuzot really could bring trouble.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: the examiner
people.about: A man checking mezuzot in Tzippori's upper market, who was caught and fined.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who taught that those on a mission for a commandment come to no harm.

people.name: Samuel
people.about: The prophet sent by God to anoint David, who feared Saul would kill him.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll of Torah verses fixed to a doorpost, as the Torah commands. Public ones on city gates were checked from time to time.
A silver coin; a thousand zuz was a very large sum.

yoma-12b-12-12.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of Yosef ben Elem of Tzippori, who was appointed to serve in place of a High Priest who had become disqualified. When the High Priest could serve again, the Sages ruled that he returns to his service. Yosef ben Elem could serve neither as High Priest, because two equal High Priests would breed hatred, nor as an ordinary priest, because in holy matters one raises a person up and does not bring him down.
yoma-12b-12-12.why: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree about a stand-in High Priest once the original returns. Rabbi Yosei cites this case to prove his view that the stand-in may serve in neither role, and the Gemara then rules like him.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who cites the incident as proof of his opinion.

people.name: Yosef ben Elem
people.about: A priest from Tzippori appointed to stand in for a disqualified High Priest.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who alone performed the Yom Kippur service and wore eight special garments; an ordinary priest wore four.
Something, such as ritual impurity, that temporarily prevented the High Priest from serving.

yoma-19b-3-4.note: A Sadducee serving as High Priest on Yom Kippur prepared the incense outside and only then carried it into the Holy of Holies, as the Sadducees held it should be done. He came out overjoyed. His father met him and said: 'My son, though we are Sadducees, we fear the Pharisees.' The son answered that all his life he had been troubled by the verse 'For I will appear in the cloud above the Ark cover,' and now that he had the chance, how could he not fulfill it? The Sages said that within a few days he died, was thrown on a garbage heap, and worms came out of his nose. Others say an angel struck him in the face as he came out, and his fellow priests found the mark of a calf's hoof between his shoulders.
yoma-19b-3-4.why: The mishna says the Elders made the High Priest swear not to change the service, and the Gemara has just explained the fear: that he would light the incense outside, as the Sadducees did. This story shows what happened when one did.

people.name: the Sadducee
people.about: A High Priest who followed the Sadducee practice with the incense on Yom Kippur.

people.name: his father
people.about: Also a Sadducee, who warned his son that they feared the Pharisees.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who taught the version in which an angel struck the High Priest.

terms.meaning: Rival groups in Second Temple times. The Pharisees followed the Sages' oral tradition; the Sadducees rejected it and read Scripture their own way.
The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, and only on Yom Kippur.
Fragrant spices burned on coals. On Yom Kippur the High Priest offered them in the Holy of Holies, where they made a cloud of smoke.
A collection of early teachings arranged like the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, filling in details it leaves out.

yoma-20b-4-5.note: Rav came to Rabbi Sheila's town, where he was not known. Rabbi Sheila had no one to repeat his lecture aloud to the public, so Rav took the job, and explained the phrase keriat hagever as 'the call of the man'. Rabbi Sheila told him to say 'the call of the rooster'. Rav answered with a saying: a flute is music to noblemen but means nothing to weavers. When I said this before Rabbi Hiyya, he raised no objection, and you correct me? Rabbi Sheila realized who he was: 'Is the Master Rav? Let the Master rest.' Rav replied: 'If you hired yourself out to him, comb his wool.' Some say he answered that in holy matters one raises a person up and does not bring him down.
yoma-20b-4-5.why: The mishna uses keriat hagever to mark a time in the Temple, and Rav and Rabbi Sheila disagree over its meaning. This story is their disagreement as it came up in a lecture; the Gemara then cites an early teaching for each side.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage, unknown in Rabbi Sheila's town, who volunteered to repeat Rabbi Sheila's lecture to the public.

people.name: Rabbi Sheila
people.about: The town's leading scholar, who corrected Rav and then recognized him.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage for whom Rav had once given the same explanation without objection.

terms.meaning: A speaker who stood beside a Sage giving a public lecture, repeating and explaining his words loudly to the audience.
A phrase from the mishna marking an early-morning time in the Temple. Gever can mean both 'man' and 'rooster'.

yoma-20b-7-7.note: King Agrippa was traveling on the road and heard the voice of Gevini the Crier, the Temple official who woke the priests each morning, from three parasangs away. When the king got home, he sent him gifts. The Gemara adds that the High Priest's voice was greater still: once, when he called out 'Please, God' in his Yom Kippur confession, he was heard in Jericho, which Rabba bar bar Hana said, quoting Rabbi Yohanan, is ten parasangs from Jerusalem.
yoma-20b-7-7.why: Rav explained the mishna's keriat hagever as 'the call of the man', and the Gemara has cited an early teaching about Gevini the Crier's call to support him. This incident shows how far that call carried.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: A king who heard the Crier's voice from far away and sent him gifts.

people.name: Gevini the Crier
people.about: A Temple official whose morning call to priests, Levites and Israelites carried three parasangs.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Quotes Rabbi Yohanan on the distance from Jerusalem to Jericho.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who said Jericho is ten parasangs from Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance; the translation puts three parasangs at slightly more than eight miles.
On Yom Kippur the High Priest laid his hands on his bull offering and confessed the sins of himself and his household aloud, calling on God's name.

yoma-22b-17-17.note: Rav Huna read the verse 'Saul was one year old when he began to reign' as meaning that Saul was as free of sin as a one-year-old. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objected: why not say he was like a one-year-old smeared with mud and excrement? That night Rav Nahman was shown a frightening dream. He said: 'I humbly submit to you, bones of Saul son of Kish.' He was shown a frightening dream again, and this time said: 'I humbly submit to you, bones of Saul son of Kish, king of Israel.'
yoma-22b-17-17.why: The Gemara is weighing the sins of Saul and David and how each was punished. Rav Nahman's dreams warn against belittling Saul, and the discussion goes on to ask why Saul's line did not keep the throne.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who mocked Rav Huna's reading of a verse about Saul and was then troubled by frightening dreams.

people.name: Saul son of Kish
people.about: The first king of Israel, whose bones Rav Nahman addressed in apology.

yoma-23a-10-12.note: Two priests were running neck and neck up the ramp to the altar. One of them reached the last four cubits first, and the other took a knife and stabbed him in the heart. Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps of the Temple's entrance hall and cried: 'Hear, my brothers of the house of Israel!' He quoted the Torah's law of a slain man found in a field and asked who must bring the heifer whose neck is broken here, the city or the Temple courts. All the people burst into tears. The boy's father came and found him still convulsing. He said: 'May he be your atonement. My son is still convulsing, so the knife has not become impure.' The Tosefta comments that the purity of vessels mattered more to them than bloodshed.
yoma-23a-10-12.why: The mishna tells of a priest whose leg was broken in this race, which led the Sages to replace it with a lottery. After this account the Gemara asks which incident came first and why the murder alone did not end the race.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who rose on the Temple steps and addressed the people after the stabbing.

people.name: the father of the boy
people.about: Father of the stabbed young priest, who worried that the knife not become impure.

terms.meaning: The sloped walkway up to the altar. Priests raced up it for the right to clear the ashes, and the first to reach within four cubits of the top won.
A rite in the Torah: when a murdered body is found and the killer is unknown, the elders of the nearest town break a young cow's neck to atone.
A state that bars a person or object from Temple use. A knife touching a dead body would become impure; while the boy lived, it would not.
A collection of early teachings arranged like the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, filling in details it leaves out.

yoma-23b-1-1.note: A young priest had been attacked and killed in the Temple during the priests' race up to the altar. His father came and found the boy still convulsing. He said: May my son's death be an atonement for you; but my son is still alive. The account concludes that the ritual purity of the Temple utensils mattered more to the people than the shedding of blood.
yoma-23b-1-1.why: The Gemara is retelling the killing of this priest and now asks what that closing comment means: had murder become trivial to them, or had purity been exaggerated? From a verse about Manasseh spilling innocent blood, it concludes that bloodshed had become trivial.

people.name: The boy's father
people.about: Father of the young priest who was attacked; he speaks over his dying son.

terms.meaning: Something that wipes away guilt or sin before God. The father bitterly offers his son's death as an atonement for the people.
Temple vessels had to be kept free of ritual impurity, which contact with a corpse would cause. The concern here is for the vessels rather than for the boy's life.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.

yoma-26b-4-4.note: On the festival of Sukkot a priest poured water on the altar. Once a priest, described in the translation as a Sadducee who rejected this rite, poured the water onto his own feet instead. All the people pelted him with their etrogim. From then on they would say to whoever poured the water: Raise your hand, so everyone could see it go onto the altar.
yoma-26b-4-4.why: The Gemara has claimed that the water was poured only with the morning offering. Rav Ashi brings this incident as support: people pelted the priest with etrogim, which they carry in the morning, so the pouring must have happened then.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who cites this incident from a mishna as proof.

terms.meaning: A rite performed on Sukkot in the Temple: water was poured on the altar alongside the usual wine.
A citrus fruit that people hold, with a palm branch, during the Sukkot prayers; plural etrogim.
A member of a Jewish group of Temple times that rejected many of the Sages' traditions, including this water rite.

yoma-35b-4-4.note: The mother of the High Priest Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum made him a tunic worth twenty thousand dinars. His fellow priests did not let him wear it, because in it he looked naked. The Gemara objects that priestly garments were woven from six-fold thread, so how could anyone see through it? Abaye answers that it was like wine in a glass cup: the fine linen let his skin show through.
yoma-35b-4-4.why: The Gemara has ruled that a priest may serve in a tunic his own mother made, once he gives it to the public. After the case of Rabbi Yishmael ben Pabi, who did just that, this is a contrasting case where the fellow priests refused the gift.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum
people.about: A High Priest whose mother made him a very costly tunic.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who explains how the tunic could be see-through.

terms.meaning: The long linen robe worn by priests in the Temple service.
A coin; twenty thousand dinars marks the tunic as extravagantly expensive.

yoma-35b-6-7.note: Every day Hillel the Elder earned half a dinar. He gave half to the guard of the study hall and lived on the other half with his family. One day he earned nothing, and the guard would not let him in. He climbed onto the roof and sat at the skylight to hear Shemaya and Avtalyon teach. It was a winter Friday and snow fell on him all night. At dawn the teachers noticed the hall was dark, saw a man's shape in the skylight, and found him under three cubits of snow. They pulled him out, washed him, rubbed him with oil and sat him by the fire, saying: This man is worthy of desecrating Shabbat for him.
yoma-35b-6-7.why: The Sages teach that in the heavenly court a poor man who says he was too busy earning a living to study Torah is asked: Were you poorer than Hillel? This story is the proof that poverty is no excuse.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: A poor laborer who pays to enter the study hall and risks his life to hear Torah.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two teachers in the study hall; he notices the hall is dark.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: Shemaya's colleague, whom Shemaya calls his brother.

terms.meaning: Friday, the day before the Sabbath; their rescue efforts at dawn fall on Shabbat itself.
A winter month in the Jewish calendar.
Do work normally forbidden on the Sabbath, such as lighting a fire. Saving a life permits this; the teachers say Hillel especially deserves it.
An ancient measure, roughly the length of a forearm, about half a meter.

yoma-35b-9-9.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum had inherited a thousand villages and a thousand ships, yet he spent his days walking from town to town to study Torah. Once his own servants came upon him, did not recognize him, and seized him for forced labor. He begged them: Please, let me go and study Torah. They answered: By the life of Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum, we will not let you go. He had never gone to see his own property; he sat and studied Torah day and night.
yoma-35b-9-9.why: The Sages teach that in the heavenly court a rich man who says he was too busy with his property to study Torah is asked: Were you richer than Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum? This story shows how little his wealth distracted him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum
people.about: A man of enormous inherited wealth who devoted himself to Torah study instead of his estates.

terms.meaning: Forced labor: being seized to work for a lord or official without pay.

yoma-38a-1-2.note: Nicanor went to Alexandria in Egypt to bring back copper doors for a Temple gate. On the voyage home a storm threatened to drown him. The passengers threw one of the heavy doors into the sea, but the storm went on. When they went to throw the second, Nicanor wrapped his arms around it and said: Throw me in with it. At once the sea calmed. He grieved for the lost door all the way, but when they reached the port of Akko it was poking out from under the side of the ship. Some say a sea creature swallowed it and spat it out onto land.
yoma-38a-1-2.why: The mishna names Nicanor among those remembered well for what they did in the Temple, saying miracles happened to his doors. This teaching spells out the miracles; the Gemara then explains that this is why his gates alone were never replaced with gold.

people.name: Nicanor
people.about: The man who brought copper doors from Alexandria for the Temple and would not give up the second one.

terms.meaning: A great city in Egypt, known for its craftsmen.
A port city on the coast of the Land of Israel.

yoma-38a-6-8.note: The House of Garmu, a family of craftsmen, knew how to make the shewbread for the Temple and refused to teach anyone. The Sages brought bakers from Alexandria instead, who could bake the bread but could not take it out of the oven as well, and their bread grew moldy. Saying that everything God created was for His glory, the Sages sent for the House of Garmu. They would not come until their wages were doubled. Asked why they had kept the secret, they said their family knew the Temple would be destroyed and feared an unworthy man would use the skill for idol worship. They were praised for this: their children never ate fine bread, so no one could say they lived off the shewbread's secret.
yoma-38a-6-8.why: The mishna lists the House of Garmu among those remembered badly for refusing to teach their craft. This teaching tells the full story, which ends by giving them a good reason and praising them.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who gives a different figure for the family's wages: twenty-four maneh, raised to forty-eight.

terms.meaning: Twelve loaves set out each week on a table in the Temple, made in a difficult shape and meant to stay fresh all week.
A large sum of money, equal to one hundred dinars.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

yoma-38a-9-11.note: The House of Avtinas knew how to prepare the Temple incense and refused to teach anyone. The Sages brought craftsmen from Alexandria who could blend the spices, but their smoke spread every which way instead of rising straight like a stick. Saying that God made everything for His sake, the Sages sent for the House of Avtinas, who came only when their wages were doubled. Asked why they kept the secret, they said their family knew the Temple would be destroyed and feared an unworthy man would use it for idol worship. They were praised: no bride from their homes ever wore perfume, and brides marrying in agreed not to, so no one could say they perfumed themselves with the incense.
yoma-38a-9-11.why: The mishna lists the House of Avtinas among those remembered badly for refusing to teach. Like the House of Garmu just before, the full story ends with a reason that wins them praise.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who gives a different figure for the family's wages: twenty-four maneh, raised to forty-eight.

terms.meaning: A blend of spices burned in the Temple every day; its smoke was meant to rise in a straight column.
A large sum of money, equal to one hundred dinars.

yoma-38a-12-12.note: Rabbi Yishmael tells that once, while walking on the road, he met a descendant of the House of Avtinas, the family that had kept the Temple incense recipe secret. He said to him: Your fathers tried to increase their own honor and lessen God's. Now God's honor stays as it was, and He has lessened theirs.
yoma-38a-12-12.why: The Gemara has just told how the House of Avtinas guarded their secret. This is the first of several meetings with the family after the Temple fell; the series ends with Rabbi Akiva ruling that they must no longer be spoken of badly.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who meets a descendant of the House of Avtinas and rebukes him.

terms.meaning: The family of craftsmen who prepared the incense for the Temple and would not teach the method to others.

yoma-38a-13-13.note: Rabbi Akiva reports what Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga told him. Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga went out to a field to gather herbs with a descendant of the House of Avtinas, and saw the man laugh and cry. He cried, he said, remembering his ancestors' honor, and laughed because God will one day restore it. What reminded him? The smoke-raising herb was right in front of him. Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga asked him to point it out. The man said: We are under an oath not to show it to anyone.
yoma-38a-13-13.why: This is one of a series of meetings with the House of Avtinas after the Temple's destruction. Here the family still guards its secret; in the next, they finally hand it over.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who passes on this account.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga
people.about: The Sage who went gathering herbs with a member of the House of Avtinas.

terms.meaning: The family of craftsmen who prepared the incense for the Temple and would not teach the method to others.
The secret ingredient that made the Temple incense smoke rise in a straight column.

yoma-38a-14-14.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri tells that he once met an old man holding a scroll. Asked where he was from, the man said: the House of Avtinas. Asked what he held, he said: a scroll of spices. When Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri asked to see it, the old man said that while his family flourished they never gave it to anyone, but now here it was, and he should take care with it. When Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri told this to Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva said: From now on it is forbidden to speak badly of them.
yoma-38a-14-14.why: This closes the series of meetings with the House of Avtinas after the Temple fell. Ben Azzai then draws a lesson from the craftsmen being called back to their posts: no one can take what God has set aside for another.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: The Sage who meets the old man and is given the scroll.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who rules, on hearing the story, that the family may no longer be spoken of badly.

terms.meaning: The family of craftsmen who prepared the incense for the Temple and would not teach the method to others.
A written record of the spices and how to blend the Temple incense.

yoma-38b-2-2.note: Ben Kamtzar had a special skill in writing: holding four quills between his fingers, he could write a four-letter word all at once. He refused to teach it to anyone. When asked why, he had no answer, unlike others who had kept their skills secret and could explain themselves. The Sages applied to those others the verse 'The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing', and to ben Kamtzar and his like 'But the name of the wicked shall rot.'
yoma-38b-2-2.why: The mishna lists Temple craftsmen who kept their skills to themselves, and the Gemara is going through them one by one; just before this it described Hugras ben Levi's secret way of singing. Next it asks what it means for a name to 'rot'.

people.name: ben Kamtzar
people.about: A Temple-era scribe with a unique writing technique that he refused to teach.

yoma-38b-3-3.note: Doeg ben Yosef's father died and left him a small child with his mother. Every day she measured his height in handbreadths and gave the Temple his weight in gold. Later, when the enemy prevailed over the city, she slaughtered him and ate him.
yoma-38b-3-3.why: Rabbi Elazar reads the verse 'the name of the wicked shall rot' to mean that no one names children after the wicked. Ravina objects with this boy, named Doeg after a wicked biblical figure; the Gemara answers: see what befell him, so the name was a bad omen.

people.name: Doeg ben Yosef
people.about: A boy left fatherless as a small child; his mother doted on him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who explains that the names of the wicked are not given to others.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rabbi Elazar with this incident.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure, the width of a hand, a few inches.

yoma-39b-2-2.note: In the year Shimon HaTzaddik died, he told his companions he would die that year. Asked how he knew, he said: every Yom Kippur an old man dressed and wrapped in white met me, went in with me and came out with me. Today an old man dressed and wrapped in black met me, went in with me, and did not come out with me. After the festival of Sukkot he was ill for seven days and died.
yoma-39b-2-2.why: The Gemara has been listing blessings that were present in the Temple and then faded. This account of the High Priest's death is followed by the signs that changed after him: the priests stopped using God's name in their blessing, and the lots stopped falling as before.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest who foresees his own death from a vision on Yom Kippur.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the one day a year the High Priest entered the innermost chamber of the Temple, the Holy of Holies.
The autumn festival of booths, which comes a few days after Yom Kippur.

yoma-39b-5-5.note: In the forty years before the Second Temple was destroyed, the signs of favor stopped: the lot for God never came up in the High Priest's right hand, the crimson wool strip no longer turned white, and the westernmost lamp of the candelabrum did not stay lit. The doors of the Sanctuary kept opening by themselves, until Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai scolded them: Sanctuary, why do you frighten yourself? I know you will be destroyed, as Zechariah prophesied, 'Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.'
yoma-39b-5-5.why: The Gemara has just told how, after the High Priest Shimon HaTzaddik died, the miracles of his time faded. This continues the decline down to the destruction; the Gemara then explains why the Temple is called Lebanon, the name in Zechariah's verse.

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Scolded the Sanctuary doors that opened by themselves, telling them he already knew the Temple would be destroyed.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest; during his tenure the lot for God always came up in his right hand.

terms.meaning: On Yom Kippur the High Priest drew lots to decide which of two goats was offered to God and which was sent to Azazel; the lot for God coming up in his right hand was taken as a good sign.
A red strip tied to the goat sent away to Azazel on Yom Kippur; its turning white was taken as a sign that the people's sins were forgiven.
One lamp of the Temple candelabrum that would miraculously stay lit longer than the others.
The main building of the Temple, which housed the inner holy rooms.

yoma-47a-10-10.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit, the High Priest, was once talking with an Arab in the market, according to the translation on Yom Kippur, when a drop of the man's spit landed on his clothes. This made him ritually impure, so his brother Yeshevav went in and served as High Priest in his place. So their mother saw two of her sons serve as High Priest on one day.
yoma-47a-10-10.why: The Gemara mentioned Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit's huge hands while explaining how the High Priest carries the coal pan and the incense, and now gathers more stories about him.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit
people.about: A High Priest made ritually impure by a stranger's spit.

people.name: Yeshevav
people.about: His brother, who served as High Priest in his place that day.

terms.meaning: A state that bars a person from Temple service until it is removed. The Sages treated a non-Jew's spit as causing it.
A man with an unusual bodily discharge, whose spit and touch cause ritual impurity.
The chief priest, who alone performed the Yom Kippur service in the Temple.

yoma-47a-11-11.note: Another time, Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit, the High Priest, went out and talked with an officer in the market, and a drop of the officer's spit landed on his clothes. His brother Yosef went in and served as High Priest in his place. Again their mother saw two of her sons serve as High Priest on one day.
yoma-47a-11-11.why: The Gemara is collecting stories about Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit. This second incident echoes the first, and leads to the teaching that all seven of his mother's sons served as High Priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit
people.about: A High Priest, again made unfit to serve by a stranger's spit.

people.name: Yosef
people.about: His brother, who served as High Priest in his place.

terms.meaning: An officer or governor.
The chief priest of the Temple. A High Priest made ritually impure could not serve, and another took his place.

yoma-47a-12-12.note: Kimhit had seven sons, and all of them served as High Priest. The Sages asked her what she had done to deserve this. She said: In all my days, the beams of my house never saw the braids of my hair. They answered: Many women did the same, and it did not help them.
yoma-47a-12-12.why: The Gemara has just told how two of Kimhit's sons each stood in for their brother as High Priest on a single day. This teaching rounds out those stories before the discussion returns to how the High Priest takes a handful of incense.

people.name: Kimhit
people.about: Mother of seven sons who all served as High Priest; the Sages ask her the reason.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who led its most important services.

yoma-53a-23-24.note: When Rabbi Yohanan left Rabbi Elazar, his student, Rabbi Elazar would bow and stand in place until his teacher was out of sight. When Rabbi Elazar was the one leaving, he would walk backward until Rabbi Yohanan could no longer see him. Rava, taking leave of his teacher Rav Yosef, would walk backward until he bruised his legs and the threshold of Rav Yosef's house was covered in blood. People told Rav Yosef, who the translation notes was blind, what Rava was doing. Rav Yosef said to him: May it be God's will that you rise to the head of the whole city.
yoma-53a-23-24.why: The mishna says the High Priest leaves the Holy of Holies walking backward. The Gemara extends this to priests, Levites and Israelites leaving the Temple, and to a student leaving his teacher; these are examples of that last rule.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A student who would not turn his back on his teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A student who walked backward from his teacher until he bled.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Rava's teacher, who blesses him when told what he does.

yoma-53b-7-7.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was walking on the road when rain began to fall on him. He said: Master of the Universe, the whole world is comfortable and Hanina is suffering. The rain stopped. When he got home he said: Master of the Universe, the whole world is suffering and Hanina is comfortable. The rain came back.
yoma-53b-7-7.why: The High Priest prayed on Yom Kippur that the prayers of travelers asking for rain to stop should not be heard. Rav Yosef uses this story to ask what good that prayer did against Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, whose words God carried out.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose prayers stop and restart the rain.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who compares Rabbi Hanina's prayer with the High Priest's.

terms.meaning: A way of addressing God in prayer.

yoma-53b-8-8.note: A High Priest once made his prayer long. His fellow priests decided to go in after him, and as they began to go in, he came out. They asked why he had prayed so long. He said: Does it trouble you that I prayed for you and for the Temple not to be destroyed? They told him not to make a habit of it, as they had learned that the High Priest did not draw out his prayer, so as not to frighten the people.
yoma-53b-8-8.why: The mishna says the High Priest kept his prayer short; this incident, taught by the Sages, shows the reason given for that rule.

terms.meaning: The chief priest, who on Yom Kippur entered the innermost room of the Temple alone and said a prayer there.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.

yoma-54a-6-7.note: Rav Nahman cites a teaching that the Ark of the Covenant was hidden in the Temple's Chamber of the Woodshed. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak backs it with a mishna: a priest at work there noticed one floor tile that looked different from the rest. He went to tell his friend, but his soul departed before he could finish, and so they knew for certain the Ark was buried there. Rabbi Helbo says the priest had been banging the floor with his axe; the school of Rabbi Yishmael says two blemished priests were sorting wood when one dropped his axe into that spot, and fire burst out and consumed him.
yoma-54a-6-7.why: The Gemara has been arguing over whether the Ark was taken away into exile, testing whether the verse's words 'there to this day' mean forever. After Ulla's proof is refuted, this account supports the Rabbis' view that the Ark never left but was hidden in the Temple.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Cites the teaching that the Ark was hidden in the Chamber of the Woodshed.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Supports that teaching with the mishna about the priest who saw the odd floor tile.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥelbo
people.about: Explains that the priest had been striking the floor with his axe.

terms.meaning: The gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the covenant and stood in the innermost room of the Temple.
A storeroom in the Temple courtyard where wood for the altar fire was kept and checked.
Priests with a physical defect, who could not serve at the altar but did other Temple work such as checking the firewood for worms.
The earliest written collection of rabbinic teachings, on which the Gemara comments.

yoma-54b-0-0.note: Reish Lakish tells what happened when gentiles entered the Temple's Sanctuary: they saw images of the cherubs clinging to one another. They carried them out to the market and mocked: these Jews, whose blessing is a blessing and whose curse is a curse, busy themselves with things like this? At once they debased them, and Reish Lakish applies the verse 'All who honored her debase her, because they have seen her nakedness.'
yoma-54b-0-0.why: The discussion has just said that the Temple walls bore carved cherubs embracing 'like a man clinging to his partner', a sign of God's love for Israel. Reish Lakish's account shows how outsiders mocked those same images.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who tells what the gentiles did when they saw the cherubs.

terms.meaning: Winged figures that stood over the Ark and were also carved on the Temple walls.
The inner building of the Temple, where only priests could enter.

yoma-59a-4-4.note: Rabbi Yishmael reports that two High Priests from the days of the First Temple were still alive. One said that when he sprinkled the blood on the inner altar he went around it by hand; the other said he walked around it on foot. Each gave a reason for what he had done. The text does not say which of them was right.
yoma-59a-4-4.why: The Gemara has been explaining a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili over how the High Priest goes around the inner altar on Yom Kippur. This report shows the same disagreement between priests who actually served; their two reasons follow in the discussion.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage who reports what the two surviving High Priests said.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who performed the special Yom Kippur service.
The small gold altar inside the Temple building, used for incense; on Yom Kippur blood was sprinkled on its corners.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

yoma-66b-6-9.note: Students put a string of questions to Rabbi Eliezer about the scapegoat: if it fell ill, could its escort carry it on his shoulder? If the escort fell ill, could someone else take it? If it was pushed off the cliff and did not die, should he go down and kill it? Each time he dodged, with answers like 'That goat can carry me and you.' The Sages say yes to all three. They asked him more: about a certain man's place in the World-to-Come, about saving a ewe or a shepherd from a lion, about a mamzer's inheritance, about plastering one's house. Each time he answered with another question.
yoma-66b-6-9.why: The Gemara has just ruled that the man sending the scapegoat may enter the Temple courtyard even if he is impure; these further scapegoat questions follow. Afterward the Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer dodged them because he never said anything he had not heard from his teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who answers each of his students' questions with an evasion or another question.

terms.meaning: On Yom Kippur one goat was sent into the wilderness carrying the people's sins, and pushed off a cliff.
The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
A child of a union the Torah forbids, such as adultery, who may not marry most other Jews.
The duty of a man to marry his brother's widow when the brother died without children.

yoma-69a-9-12.note: The Samaritans asked Alexander the Macedonian for permission to destroy the Temple, and he gave it. When Shimon HaTzaddik, the High Priest, heard, he put on the priestly vestments and set out with the nobles of Israel carrying torches; they marched all night toward Alexander's camp. At dawn Alexander saw Shimon, got down from his chariot and bowed to him, saying this man's image led him to victory in his battles. Hearing that the Samaritans wanted to destroy the house where the Jews prayed for him and his kingdom, Alexander handed the Samaritans over to them. They stabbed them in their heels, dragged them behind horses to Mount Gerizim, plowed it and sowed it with leeks, and made that day a festival.
yoma-69a-9-12.why: The Gemara has quoted a ruling that priestly vestments may not be worn outside the Temple. This story, in which Shimon HaTzaddik wears them on the road, challenges that ruling; the Gemara answers that they were only vestment-like garments, or that a time of danger allowed it.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: The High Priest, who goes out in the priestly vestments to meet Alexander.

people.name: Alexander the Macedonian
people.about: The king who first allows the Temple's destruction, then bows to Shimon HaTzaddik.

terms.meaning: A people living in the land of Israel, rivals of the Jews, who had their own temple on Mount Gerizim.
The sacred garments the priests wore for the Temple service.
The mountain where the Samaritans had their temple.
A town on the road where the two groups met at sunrise.

yoma-71b-1-2.note: A High Priest came out of the Temple and all the people followed him. When they saw Shemaya and Avtalyon, the heads of the Sanhedrin, they left him and walked after them instead. Later, when Shemaya and Avtalyon came to take leave of him, he said: 'Let the descendants of the gentile nations come in peace', mocking their descent from converts. They answered: Let the descendants of the nations come in peace, who act as Aaron did, and let not a descendant of Aaron come in peace, who does not act as Aaron did.
yoma-71b-1-2.why: The mishna describes the people escorting the High Priest home after Yom Kippur, where he made a feast for his loved ones. This incident shows a time the crowd left the High Priest for the Sages.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two heads of the Sanhedrin, descended from converts according to the text.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: Shemaya's colleague, also a head of the Sanhedrin and of convert descent.

people.name: High Priest
people.about: An unnamed High Priest who mocks the two Sages when the crowd follows them instead of him.

terms.meaning: The highest court and council of Sages.
Moses' brother, the first High Priest, remembered for loving and pursuing peace; all priests descend from him.

yoma-75b-7-7.note: Rav Yehuda found quail among his wine barrels, and Rav Hisda found quail among the logs in his storeroom. Every day Rava's sharecropper brought him a quail. One day he brought none, and Rava wondered why. He went up to the roof and heard a child reciting: 'When I heard, my innards trembled.' Rava concluded that Rav Hisda had died, since it is on account of the teacher that the student eats.
yoma-75b-7-7.why: The Gemara has been describing the quail the Israelites ate in the desert, how small and how rich it was. It moves on to quail that later Sages found as a gift.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who found quail among his wine barrels.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who found quail among his logs; Rava's teacher, whose death Rava understands from the missing quail.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Hisda's student, whose sharecropper brought him a quail every day.

terms.meaning: A small game bird; the Torah tells that God sent quail to the Israelites in the desert.
A tenant who works another man's fields in exchange for part of the crop.

yoma-78a-4-5.note: The Exilarch came to give a lecture at Rav Natan's study hall in Hagronya. Rafram and all the Sages came; Ravina did not. The next day Rafram, wanting to clear Ravina in the Exilarch's eyes, asked him why he had stayed away. Ravina said his foot hurt. Rafram said he should have worn shoes; Ravina said it was the back of his foot. Then sandals? There was a pool of water on the way. Then cross it in sandals? Ravina replied: does the Master not hold with Rav Ashi, who said one should not cross water in sandals in the first place?
yoma-78a-4-5.why: The Gemara has been asking whether one may cross water on Shabbat in shoes or sandals, and Rav Ashi has just ruled that one should not set out to do so in sandals. Ravina's excuse turns on exactly that ruling.

people.name: Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who came to give the lecture.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: A Sage who attended, and questions Ravina to clear him before the Exilarch.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who missed the lecture and explains why.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose ruling about crossing water in sandals Ravina cites.

terms.meaning: Latin for 'from the start': doing something in the first place, as opposed to accepting it after the fact.

yoma-78a-8-8.note: Ze'eira bar Hama, who had hosted Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and all the Sages of Caesarea, said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son Rav Yosef: 'Son of a lion, let me tell you a fine thing your father used to do.' On the day before Yom Kippur he soaked a cloth in water and wrung it until it was almost dry, and the next day wiped his face, hands and feet with it. On the day before the Ninth of Av he soaked the cloth, and the next day passed it over his eyes.
yoma-78a-8-8.why: The Gemara has been listing how Sages cooled themselves on Yom Kippur without breaking the ban on bathing. Right after, Rabba bar Mari gives the reverse version of the custom, and the Gemara notes that wringing a cloth is itself forbidden on Yom Kippur.

people.name: Ze'eira bar Ḥama
people.about: The host of many Sages, who tells Rav Yosef about his father's custom.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, to whom the custom is told.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage whose custom with the damp cloth is described.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, a fast day on which eating, drinking and bathing are forbidden.
A fast day mourning the Temple's destruction; the text notes its ban on bathing is a rabbinic rule, not a Torah law.

yoma-81b-10-10.note: Rav Giddel bar Menashe of Birei DeNeresh taught in a public lecture that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The next year everyone went out, mixed vinegar with water and drank it on Yom Kippur. Rav Giddel heard and became angry. He said: I said one is not liable only after the fact; did I say it may be drunk in the first place? I spoke of a little; did I say a lot? I spoke of pure vinegar; did I say anything about diluted?
yoma-81b-10-10.why: The mishna implies that drinking vinegar on Yom Kippur makes one liable, following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who says vinegar revives the spirit and counts as a drink. The story shows how a public ruling against his view was misread.

people.name: Rav Giddel bar Menashe
people.about: The Sage who taught that the law does not follow Rabbi, then rebuked those who misread him.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose view that vinegar counts as a drink Rav Giddel rejected.

terms.meaning: Held guilty of breaking the fast, with the penalty that carries.
Latin for 'from the start': doing something in the first place, as opposed to accepting it after the fact.

yoma-82b-1-1.note: A pregnant woman smelled food on Yom Kippur and craved it. People came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who told them to whisper to her that it was Yom Kippur. They whispered to her, and it worked. Rabbi applied to her unborn child the verse 'Before I formed you in the belly I knew you', and the child born to her was Rabbi Yohanan.
yoma-82b-1-1.why: The discussion turns to a pregnant woman who smells food on Yom Kippur. Right after, a second case is told in which the same whisper fails and the child grows up wicked, so the two stories are a pair.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who tells them to whisper to the woman that it is Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The child born to that woman.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, a full day's fast from food and drink.

yoma-82b-2-2.note: Another pregnant woman smelled food on Yom Kippur and craved it. People came to Rabbi Hanina, who told them to whisper to her that it was Yom Kippur. They whispered, but she did not accept it and went on craving. Rabbi Hanina applied to her unborn child the verse 'The wicked are estranged from the womb', and the child born to her was Shabbetai, the hoarder of fruit, who held back fruit in famine years to raise its price.
yoma-82b-2-2.why: It is paired with the story just before, where the same whisper worked and the child became Rabbi Yohanan. Next the Gemara turns to the mishna's rule on feeding a sick person on Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage consulted about the pregnant woman's craving.

people.name: Shabbetai
people.about: The child born to her, known as the hoarder of fruits.

terms.meaning: Someone who bought up and held back food in famine years to drive up the price, at the cost of the poor.

yoma-83b-9-9.note: Rav Nahman, citing Shmuel, says that a person seized with bulmos should be fed a sheep's tail with honey; Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua adds fine wheat flour with honey, and Rav Pappa even barley flour with honey. Rabbi Yohanan tells that once he was seized with bulmos and ran to the east side of a fig tree, where the figs ripen first, and so fulfilled the verse 'Wisdom preserves the lives of those who have it.' Rav Yosef taught that one who wants the taste of a fig should turn to its east side.
yoma-83b-9-9.why: The Gemara has been discussing what to feed someone seized with bulmos, the dangerous hunger for which eating is allowed even on Yom Kippur. A baraita said honey and sweet foods restore his sight, and Abaye said sweets help only after other food.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Says, through Rav Nahman, to feed a sheep's tail with honey.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Reports Shmuel's remedy.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Adds fine wheat flour with honey.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Says even barley flour with honey helps.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Tells how he once ran to the east side of a fig tree when seized with bulmos.

terms.meaning: A sudden ravenous faintness that dims the eyes and can endanger life; the sufferer must be fed at once.

terms.term: east side of a fig tree
terms.meaning: The figs facing the sunrise ripen first, so that is where to find ripe fruit.

yoma-83b-10-10.note: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were walking on the road when Rabbi Yehuda was seized with bulmos. He overpowered a shepherd and ate his bread. Rabbi Yosei told him: you have robbed that shepherd. When they reached the city, Rabbi Yosei was seized with bulmos, and the townspeople surrounded him with jugs and plates. Rabbi Yehuda said to him: I robbed only the shepherd, but you have robbed the whole city.
yoma-83b-10-10.why: The Gemara has been listing remedies for bulmos, the dangerous hunger that allows eating even on Yom Kippur. This story shows two Sages struck by it, and afterward the Gemara tells another story about the same travellers.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Seized with bulmos on the road, he takes a shepherd's bread.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: His companion, who scolds him and is then seized with bulmos himself in the city.

terms.meaning: A sudden ravenous faintness that can endanger life; the sufferer must be fed at once.

yoma-83b-11-14.note: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were travelling. Rabbi Meir read people's character from their names; the others did not. Their innkeeper's name was Kidor, which Rabbi Meir linked to the verse 'a generation of upheavals'. On Friday afternoon the other two left their purses with the innkeeper, but Rabbi Meir hid his at the grave of the innkeeper's father. The father appeared to the innkeeper in a dream and told him to take the purse there; told of the dream, the Sages said Friday-twilight dreams mean nothing, but Rabbi Meir guarded his money all day and then took it. The innkeeper denied ever getting the other purses. The Sages got him drunk, saw lentils on his mustache, and gave that sign to his wife, who handed the purses over. He went and killed his wife.
yoma-83b-11-14.why: It follows the story of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on the road. Afterward the Gemara ties it to a teaching that neglecting the washing after a meal can lead to killing: had the innkeeper washed his mouth, the lentils would not have shown.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who reads character from names and does not trust the innkeeper.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A travelling companion who leaves his purse with the innkeeper.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The other companion, who also leaves his purse.

people.name: Kidor
people.about: The innkeeper, who denies receiving the purses and kills his wife.

terms.meaning: The time between sunset and dark on Friday, as Shabbat begins; the Sages say dreams then have no meaning.
A money pouch, left with the innkeeper for safekeeping over Shabbat, when money may not be carried.

yoma-84a-3-4.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan suffered from a disease called tzefidna and went to a gentile noblewoman known as a healer. She prepared a remedy for him on Thursday and Friday. He asked what he would do on Shabbat; she said he would not need it, and when he pressed her, she made him swear not to reveal the remedy. He swore, 'To the God of the Jews, I will not reveal it.' She told him, and he went out and taught it publicly.
yoma-84a-3-4.why: The mishna cites Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash allowing medicine to be put in the mouth of someone with throat pain on Shabbat. The Gemara then asks how Rabbi Yoḥanan could break his oath, and later explains he could treat this ailment on Shabbat because it spreads to the intestines and is dangerous.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage suffering from tzefidna who learned a healer's secret remedy under oath and then taught it publicly.

people.name: the matron
people.about: A gentile noblewoman healer who treated Rabbi Yoḥanan and made him swear not to reveal her remedy.

terms.meaning: An illness that starts in the teeth and gums, with bleeding, and moves on to the intestines.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, when preparing medicine is normally forbidden unless life is in danger.

yoma-85a-12-14.note: Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya were walking on the road, with Levi HaSadar and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya behind them, when they were asked how we know that saving a life overrides Shabbat. Rabbi Yishmael argued from the burglar who may be killed even though it is unclear he came to kill. Rabbi Akiva argued from the murderer-priest who is taken even off the altar if he can testify to save a life: if the Temple service, which overrides Shabbat, gives way to a doubtful chance of saving a life, all the more so does Shabbat. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argued: if circumcision, which concerns one limb, overrides Shabbat, all the more so does saving the whole body.
yoma-85a-12-14.why: The Gemara has been ruling on clearing rubble from a person trapped on Shabbat. It now seeks the source for setting Shabbat aside to save a life; more proofs follow, and Rava says only Shmuel's proof, 'and live by them', cannot be refuted.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Argues from the case of the burglar breaking in.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Argues from the priest taken from the altar to save a life.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Argues from circumcision, which overrides Shabbat.

people.name: Levi HaSadar
people.about: A younger Sage walking behind the three.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Also walking behind the elder Sages.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater: if something holds in a light case, it holds all the more in a weighty one.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest on which work is forbidden.
God's presence dwelling among the people of Israel.

yoma-87a-13-13.note: Rabbi Yirmeya had offended Rabbi Abba, and went and sat at the threshold of Rabbi Abba's house to beg forgiveness. Rabbi Abba's maid poured out dirty water and it landed on Rabbi Yirmeya's head. He said, 'They have made me into a trash heap', and applied to himself the verse 'Who lifts up the needy out of the trash heap.' Rabbi Abba heard, came out to him, and said: now I must go out to appease you, as it is written, 'Go, humble yourself and urge your neighbor.'
yoma-87a-13-13.why: Rabbi Yitzhak has just taught that one who angers a friend, even by words, must appease him, from the same verse Rabbi Abba quotes. The story shows the obligation turning around once the apologizer is himself insulted.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Offended Rabbi Abba and sat at his door to seek forgiveness.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The offended Sage, who ends up seeking to appease Rabbi Yirmeya.

terms.meaning: To ask forgiveness of someone you have wronged until they are reconciled.

yoma-87a-15-15.note: A butcher had insulted Rav and did not come to apologize. On the eve of Yom Kippur Rav said he would go and make peace with him. On the way he met Rav Huna, who asked where he was going; when Rav told him, Rav Huna said, 'Abba is going to kill a person.' Rav went and stood before the butcher, who was splitting an animal's head. The butcher looked up and said, 'Are you Abba? Go, I have nothing to say to you.' As he split the head, a bone flew out, struck him in the throat, and killed him.
yoma-87a-15-15.why: The Gemara has been teaching how one must seek forgiveness, especially before Yom Kippur, and has just told how Rabbi Zeira made himself available to anyone who had wronged him. Here Rav goes further and seeks out the man who wronged him.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage, called Abba here, who goes to make peace with the butcher who insulted him.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rav's student, who predicts that the visit will cost the butcher his life.

people.name: butcher
people.about: An unnamed man who insulted Rav and refuses to make peace.

terms.meaning: The day before the Day of Atonement, when people seek forgiveness from those they have wronged.

yoma-87a-16-16.note: Rav was reading the Torah portion aloud before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Each time a senior scholar walked in, Rabbi Ḥiyya, then bar Kappara, then Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi, he started again from the beginning. When Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama came in, Rav decided not to start over again, and Rabbi Ḥanina was offended. For thirteen years Rav went to him on the eve of Yom Kippur to ask forgiveness, and he would not be appeased. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ḥanina had dreamt of Rav hung on a palm tree, a sign he would head a yeshiva, so he refused, so that Rav would go to study Torah in Babylonia.
yoma-87a-16-16.why: The Gemara is telling stories of Sages seeking forgiveness on Yom Kippur eve. It asks how Rav could ask more than the three times Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina sets, and how Rabbi Ḥanina could refuse, given Rava's teaching that one who forgives is forgiven.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Read the Torah portion before Rabbi and, for not restarting for Rabbi Ḥanina, sought his forgiveness for thirteen years.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the Torah portion was being read before him.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The first scholar to enter, for whom Rav restarted the reading; the translation calls him Rav's uncle and teacher.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A scholar who came in next; Rav restarted the reading for him too.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama
people.about: Was offended when Rav did not restart for him, and refused to be appeased because of a dream about Rav.

terms.meaning: The day before the Day of Atonement, when people traditionally ask forgiveness of those they have wronged.
The leader of an academy of Torah study.

yoma-87b-2-2.note: Rav had offended Rabbi Ḥanina by not restarting a Torah reading for him, and for thirteen years Rav came to him every Yom Kippur eve to ask forgiveness, but Rabbi Ḥanina refused. The Gemara asks how Rav could ask more than three times, against the teaching of Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, and answers that Rav was different. It then asks how Rabbi Ḥanina could refuse, when Rava taught that whoever lets go of his honor is forgiven his sins. The answer: Rabbi Ḥanina had dreamed that Rav was hung on a palm tree, a sign that he would become head of an academy, so he refused to be appeased, so that Rav would go and study Torah in Babylonia.
yoma-87b-2-2.why: The Gemara has been telling how Rav sought forgiveness from people on Yom Kippur eve; these questions explain why Rav kept asking and why Rabbi Ḥanina kept refusing, before it turns to the laws of confession on that day.
